title: The Death of Death in the Death of Christ
author: John Owen
description: John Owen examines the purpose and effects of Christ’s death. He argues that Christ’s sacrifice secures salvation for the people God has chosen, and answers arguments for universal redemption.

paragraphs.original: To the Right Honourable Robert, Earl of Warwick, etc.
paragraphs.modern: To the Right Honourable Robert, Earl of Warwick, etc.

paragraphs.original: My Lord,
paragraphs.modern: My Lord,

paragraphs.original: It is not for the benefit of any protection to the ensuing treatise, — let it stand or fall as it shall be found in the judgments of men; nor that I might take advantage to set forth any of that worth and honour which, being personal, have truly ennobled your lordship, and made a way for the delivering over of your family unto posterity with an eminent lustre added to the roll of your worthy progenitors, — which, if by myself desired, my unfitness to perform must needs render unacceptable in the performance; neither yet have I the least desire to attempt a farther advancement of myself into your lordship’s favour, being much beneath what I have already received, and fully resolved to own no other esteem among the sons of men but what shall be accounted due (be it more or less) to the discharge of my duty to my master, Jesus Christ, whose wholly I would be; — it is not all, nor one of these, nor any such as these, the usual subjects and ends of dedications, real or pretended, that prevailed upon me unto this boldness of prefixing your honoured name to this ensuing treatise (which yet, for the matter’s sake contained in it, I cannot judge unworthy of any Christian eye); but only that I might take the advantage to testify (as I do) to all the world the answering of my heart unto that obligation which your lordship was pleased to put upon me, in the undeserved, undesired favour of opening that door wherewith you are intrusted, to give me an entrance to that place for the preaching of the gospel whither I was directed by the providence of the Most High, and where I was sought by his people. In which place this I dare say, by the grace of God, that such a stock of prayers and thankfulness as your heart, which hath learned to value the least of Christ, in whomsoever it be, will not despise, is tendered to and for your lordship, even on his behalf who is less than the least of all the saints of God, and unworthy the name which yet he is bold to subscribe himself by, — Your honour’s most obliged servant in the service of Jesus Christ,
paragraphs.modern: I have not placed your honoured name before this treatise to gain your protection for it. Let it stand or fall according to the judgment people make of it. Nor am I taking this opportunity to celebrate the personal worth and honour that have truly ennobled you and added new distinction to the record of your worthy ancestors, so that your family's name will pass with greater glory to future generations. Even if I wished to attempt that, my inability to do it properly would make the result unacceptable. Nor do I have the slightest wish to win more of your favour. I am far less deserving than the favours I have already received would suggest. I am fully determined to accept no reputation among people beyond whatever, great or small, is rightly due to the way I fulfil my duty to my master, Jesus Christ, to whom I wish to belong entirely. None of these motives, nor all of them together, nor any similar purpose commonly claimed or actually pursued in dedications, has led me to take the liberty of putting your honoured name before this treatise. Nevertheless, because of its subject, I cannot consider the work unworthy of any Christian's attention. My only purpose is to tell the whole world how deeply my heart acknowledges the obligation you have placed me under. Without my deserving or requesting it, you kindly opened the door entrusted to your care and admitted me to a position in which I could preach the gospel. The providence of the Most High had directed me there, and his people had sought me out. By God's grace, I dare say that in that place prayers and gratitude are offered to you and for you in such abundance that your heart will not despise them. You have learned to value even the smallest evidence of Christ, in whomever it appears. Those prayers and thanks are offered also on behalf of someone who is less than the least of all God's saints, and unworthy of the title under which he nevertheless dares to sign himself: Your honour's deeply indebted servant in the service of Jesus Christ,

paragraphs.original: John Owen.
paragraphs.modern: John Owen.

paragraphs.original: Reader,
paragraphs.modern: Reader,

paragraphs.original: If thou intendest to go any farther, I would entreat thee to stay here a little. If thou art, as many in this pretending age, a sign or title gazer, and comest into books as Cato into the theatre, to go out again, — thou hast had thy entertainment; farewell! With him that resolves a serious view of the following discourse, and really desireth satisfaction from the word and Christian reason, about the great things contained therein, I desire a few words in the portal. Divers things there are of no small consideration to the business we have in hand, which I am persuaded thou canst not be unacquainted with; and therefore I will not trouble thee with a needless repetition of them.
paragraphs.modern: If you intend to read further, please pause here for a moment. If, like many people in this age of pretence, you only look at signs and titles, entering books as Cato entered the theatre, simply to leave again, you have had your entertainment. Farewell! But if you intend to examine the following discussion seriously, and really want answers from Scripture and Christian reasoning about the great matters it contains, I would like a few words with you at the entrance. Several things of considerable importance to our subject must already be familiar to you, I believe, so I will not trouble you by repeating them unnecessarily.

paragraphs.original: I shall only crave thy leave to preface a little to the point in hand, and my present undertaking therein, with the result of some of my thoughts concerning the whole, after a more than seven-years’ serious inquiry (bottomed, I hope, upon the strength of Christ, and guided by his Spirit) into the mind of God about these things, with a serious perusal of all which I could attain that the wit of man, in former or latter days, hath published in opposition to the truth; which I desire, according to the measure of the gift received, here to assert. Some things, then, as to the chief point in hand I would desire the reader to observe; as, —
paragraphs.modern: I ask only your permission to introduce the subject and my present treatment of it by sharing some conclusions from my reflections on the whole question. For more than seven years I have seriously investigated God's mind on these matters, relying, I hope, on Christ's strength and the guidance of his Spirit. I have also carefully read everything I could obtain that human ingenuity, in earlier or more recent times, has published against the truth I now seek to defend, according to the measure of the gift I have received. Concerning the central issue, then, I ask the reader to observe the following things:

paragraphs.original: First, That the assertion of universal redemption, or the general ransom, so as to make it in the least measure beneficial for the end intended, goes not alone. Election of free grace, as the fountain of all following dispensations, all discriminating purposes of the Almighty, depending on his own good pleasure and will, must be removed out of the way. Hence, those who would for the present (“populo ut placerent, quas fecere fabulas,”) desirously retain some show of asserting the liberty of eternally distinguishing free grace, do themselves utterly raze, in respect of any fruit or profitable issue, the whole imaginary fabric of general redemption, which they had before erected. Some of these make the decree of election to be “antecedaneous to the death of Christ” (as themselves absurdly speak), or the decree of the death of Christ: then frame a twofold election;[1] — one, of some to be the sons; the other, of the rest to be servants. But this election of some to be servants the Scripture calls reprobation, and speaks of it as the issue of hatred, or a purpose of rejection, Rom. ix. 11–13. To be a servant, in opposition to children and their liberty, is as high a curse as can be expressed, Gen. ix. 25. Is this Scripture election? Besides, if Christ died to bring those he died for unto the adoption and inheritance of children, what good could possibly redound to them thereby who were predestinated before to be only servants? Others[2] make a general conditionate decree of redemption to be antecedaneous to election; which they assert to be the first discriminating purpose concerning the sons of men, and to depend on the alone good pleasure of God. That any others shall partake of the death of Christ or the fruits thereof, either unto grace or glory, but only those persons so elected, that they deny. “Cui bono” now? To what purpose serves the general ransom, but only to assert that Almighty God would have the precious blood of his dear Son poured out for innumerable souls whom he will not have to share in any drop thereof, and so, in respect of them, to be spilt in vain, or else to be shed for them only that they might be the deeper damned? This fountain, then, of free grace, this foundation of the new covenant, this bottom of all gospel dispensations, this fruitful womb of all eternally distinguishing mercies, the purpose of God according to election, must be opposed, slighted, blasphemed, that the figment of the sons of men may not appear to be “truncus ficulnus, inutile lignum,” — an unprofitable stock; and all the thoughts of the Most High, differencing between man and man, must be made to take “occasion,” say some, to be “caused,” say others, by their holy, self-spiritual endeavours. “Gratum opus agricolis,” — a savoury sacrifice to the Roman Belus, a sacred orgie to the long-bewailed manes of St Pelagius.
paragraphs.modern: First, the claim of universal redemption, or a ransom for everyone, cannot stand alone if it is to provide even the smallest benefit toward its intended purpose. Election by free grace, the source of all God's subsequent dealings with us, must be cleared out of the way, along with every purpose of the Almighty that distinguishes between people according to his own pleasure and will. Consequently, some who want for the moment to retain an appearance of affirming the freedom of God's eternally distinguishing grace themselves demolish the imaginary structure of universal redemption they previously built, so far as any beneficial result is concerned: “populo ut placerent, quas fecere fabulas,” meaning “so that the stories they invented might please the people.” Some make the decree of election “prior to the death of Christ,” as they absurdly express it, or prior to the decree of Christ's death. They then invent two kinds of election:[1] some are chosen to be sons, and the rest to be servants. But Scripture calls this choosing of some to be servants reprobation, or rejection, and describes it as the result of hatred or a purpose to reject them, Romans 9:11–13. To be a servant, as opposed to a child enjoying a child's freedom, is as severe a curse as language can express, Genesis 9:25. Is this what Scripture means by election? Besides, if Christ died to bring those for whom he died into the adoption and inheritance of children, what possible benefit could his death bring to people already predestined to be only servants? Others[2] place a general, conditional decree of redemption before election. They say that election is God's first purpose that distinguishes between people, and that it depends entirely on his good pleasure. They deny that anyone except those elected in this way will share in Christ's death or its benefits, whether in grace or in glory. “Cui bono,” then: “For whose benefit?” What purpose does this universal ransom serve? It amounts only to saying that Almighty God wanted his dear Son's precious blood poured out for countless souls whom he does not intend to let share in a single drop of it. As far as they are concerned, it was therefore either spilled in vain or shed only to bring them a deeper condemnation. Thus God's purpose of election, the fountain of free grace, the foundation of the new covenant, the basis of all his dealings through the gospel, and the fruitful womb of every mercy that eternally distinguishes one person from another, must be opposed, belittled, and blasphemed. Otherwise this human invention would be exposed as “truncus ficulnus, inutile lignum,” “a fig-tree stump, useless wood.” Every intention of the Most High that distinguishes one person from another must, some say, take its occasion from people's own supposedly holy, spiritual efforts; others say it must actually be caused by them. “Gratum opus agricolis,” “a work welcome to farmers”: a pleasing sacrifice to Rome's Belus, a sacred rite for the long-lamented spirit of Saint Pelagius.

paragraphs.original: And here, secondly, free-will, “amor et deliciæ humani generis,” corrupted nature’s deformed darling, the Pallas or beloved self-conception of darkened minds, finds open hearts and arms for its adulterous embraces; yea, the die being cast, and Rubicon passed over, “eo devenere fata ecclesiæ,” that having opposed the free distinguishing grace of God as the sole sworn enemy thereof, it advanceth itself, or an inbred native ability in every one to embrace a portion of generally exposed mercy, under the name of free grace. “Tantane nos tenuit generis fiducia vestri?” This, this is Universalists’ free grace, which in the Scripture phrase is cursed, corrupted nature. Neither can it otherwise be. A general ransom without free-will is but “phantasiæ inutile pondus,” — “a burdensome fancy;” the merit of the death of Christ being to them as an ointment in a box, that hath neither virtue nor power to act or reach out its own application unto particulars, being only set out in the gospel to the view of all, that those who will, by their own strength, lay hold on it and apply it to themselves may be healed. Hence the dear esteem and high valuation which this old idol free-will hath attained in these days, being so useful to the general ransom that it cannot live a day without it. Should it pass for true what the Scripture affirms, namely, that we are by nature “dead in trespasses and sins,” etc., there would not be left of the general ransom a shred to take fire from the hearth. Like the wood of the vine, it would not yield a pin to hang a garment upon: all which you shall find fully declared in the ensuing treatise. But here, as though all the undertakings and Babylonish attempts of the old Pelagians, with their varnished offspring, the late Arminians, were slight and easy, I shall show you greater abominations than these, and farther discoveries of the imagery of the hearts of the sons of men. In pursuance of this persuasion of universal redemption, not a few have arrived (whither it naturally leads them) to deny the satisfaction and merit of Christ. Witness P― H―, who, not being able to untie, ventured boldly to cut this Gordian knot, but so as to make both ends of the chain useless. To the question, Whether Christ died for all men or no? he answers, “That he died neither for all nor any, so as to purchase life and salvation for them.” Ὦ τᾶν ποῖόν σε ἔπος φύγεν ἕρκος ὀδόντων; Shall cursed Socinianism be worded into a glorious discovery of free grace? Ask now for proofs of this assertion, as you might justly expect Achillean arguments from those who delight ἀκίνητα κινεῖν, and throw down such foundations (as shall put all the righteous in the world to a loss thereby), “Projicit ampullas et sesquipedalia verba,” ὑπέρογκα ματαιότητος, great swelling words of vanity, drummy expressions, a noise from emptiness, the usual language of men who know not what they speak, nor whereof they do affirm, is all that is produced. Such contemptible products have our tympanous mountains! Poor creatures, whose souls are merchandised by the painted faces of novelty and vanity, whilst these Joabs salute you with the kisses of free grace, you see not the sword that is in their hands, whereby they smite you under the fifth rib, in the very heart-blood of faith and all Christian consolation. It seems our blessed Redeemer’s deep humiliation, in bearing the chastisement of our peace and the punishment of our transgressions, being made a curse and sin, deserted under wrath and the power of death, procuring redemption and the remission of sins through the effusion of his blood, offering himself up a sacrifice to God, to make reconciliation and purchase an atonement, his pursuing this undertaking with continued intercession in the holy of holies, with all the benefits of his mediatorship, do no way procure either life and salvation or remission of sins, but only serve to declare that we are not indeed what his word affirms we are, — namely, cursed, guilty, defiled, and only not actually cast into hell. “Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?” See this at large confuted, lib. iii. Now, this last assertion, thoroughly fancied, hath opened a door and given an inlet to all those pretended heights and new-named glorious attainments which have metamorphosed the person and mediation of Christ into an imaginary diffused goodness and love, communicated from the Creator unto the new creation; than which familistical fables Cerdon’s two principles were not more absurd; the Platonic numbers nor the Valentinian Æones,[3] flowing from the teeming wombs of Πλήρωμα, Αἰών, Τέλειος, Βυθός, Σιγή, and the rest, vented for high glorious attainments in Christian religion, near fifteen hundred years ago, were not less intelligible. Neither did the corroding of Scriptures by that Pontic vermin Marcion equalize the contempt and scorn cast upon them by these impotent impostors, exempting their whispered discoveries from their trial, and exalting their revelations above their authority. Neither do some stay here; but “his gradibus itur in cœlum,” heaven itself is broke open for all. From universal redemption, through universal justification, in a general covenant, they have arrived (“haud ignota loquor”) at universal salvation; neither can any forfeiture be made of the purchased inheritance.
paragraphs.modern: And here, secondly, free will finds hearts and arms open to its adulterous embrace. It is “amor et deliciæ humani generis,” “the love and delight of the human race,” the deformed darling of corrupt human nature, the Pallas that darkened minds have conceived and lovingly brought forth themselves. Indeed, the die is cast and the Rubicon crossed. “eo devenere fata ecclesiæ,” “the fortunes of the church have come to this”: free will has attacked God's freely distinguishing grace as its one sworn enemy, and now advances itself under the name of free grace. By this it means an ability supposedly born into everyone to take a share of mercy offered generally to all. “Tantane nos tenuit generis fiducia vestri?” “Did we place such great confidence in your race?” This is the free grace of those who teach universal redemption: what Scripture calls cursed, corrupt human nature. It cannot be otherwise. A universal ransom without free will is only “phantasiæ inutile pondus,” “a useless burden of imagination.” In their account, the merit of Christ's death is like ointment kept in a box. It has no power to act or to bring about its own application to particular people. The gospel merely displays it to everyone, so that those willing to take it by their own strength and apply it to themselves may be healed. This explains the fond regard and high value now given to that old idol, free will. It is so necessary to universal ransom that the latter cannot survive a day without it. If Scripture's declaration that we are by nature “dead in our offences and sins” were accepted as true, not a scrap of universal ransom would remain fit even to carry fire from the hearth. Like vine wood, it would not supply a peg on which to hang a garment. All this is fully explained in the following treatise. But as though the projects and Babel-like ambitions of the ancient Pelagians and their polished offspring, the modern Arminians, were trivial things, I will show you greater abominations and further revelations of the idols people imagine in their hearts. By following the belief in universal redemption, quite a few have reached its natural destination: denying that Christ made satisfaction for sin or earned salvation. Take P― H―. Unable to untie this Gordian knot, he boldly cut it, but in doing so made both ends of the chain useless. Asked whether Christ died for everyone, he answers that Christ died neither for everyone nor for anyone in the sense of purchasing life and salvation for them. “Ὦ τᾶν ποῖόν σε ἔπος φύγεν ἕρκος ὀδόντων;” “My friend, what a word has escaped the fence of your teeth!” Can a change of language turn cursed Socinianism into a glorious discovery of free grace? Ask for proof of this claim. You might reasonably expect arguments as mighty as Achilles from people who delight “ἀκίνητα κινεῖν,” “to move what cannot be moved,” and who tear down foundations whose loss would leave all the world's righteous people at a loss. Instead, all they produce is “Projicit ampullas et sesquipedalia verba,” “he pours out bombast and words a foot and a half long”; “ὑπέρογκα ματαιότητος,” “swollen words of emptiness.” Grandiose phrases, hollow drumming, noise coming from emptiness: these are the usual language of people who understand neither what they say nor what they confidently assert. What contemptible offspring our swollen mountains produce! Poor people, your souls are being traded through the painted attractions of novelty and vanity. These Joabs greet you with kisses of free grace, while you fail to see the sword in their hands. With it they strike beneath your ribs, into the very lifeblood of faith and all Christian comfort. On this account, it seems, none of our blessed Redeemer's work secures life, salvation, or forgiveness of sins. Not his profound humiliation, bearing the punishment that brings us peace and the penalty for our transgressions; not his being made a curse and sin, abandoned under wrath and death's power; not his obtaining redemption and forgiveness by pouring out his blood; not his offering himself as a sacrifice to God to bring reconciliation and secure atonement; not his continuing this work by constant intercession in the holy of holies; not any benefit of his work as mediator. All of it supposedly serves only to show that we are not really what his word says we are: cursed, guilty, defiled, and lacking only our actual casting into hell. “Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?” This is refuted at length in Book III. Thoroughly embraced, this last claim has opened the door to all those supposedly lofty, newly celebrated spiritual achievements that turn Christ's person and mediation into an imagined, widely diffused goodness and love, communicated by the Creator to the new creation. Cerdon's two principles were no more absurd than these fables of the Familists. Nor were the Platonic numbers or the Valentinian Æones, meaning “Aeons,”[3] any less intelligible. Those Aeons flowed from the fertile wombs of Πλήρωμα, “Fullness”; Αἰών, “Aeon” or “Eternity”; Τέλειος, “Perfect”; Βυθός, “Depth”; Σιγή, “Silence”; and the rest. Nearly fifteen hundred years ago these too were presented as lofty, glorious achievements in Christianity. Even the damage done to Scripture by that vermin from Pontus, Marcion, did not equal the contempt these powerless impostors show it. They exempt their whispered discoveries from its examination and place their revelations above its authority. Some do not stop even here. “his gradibus itur in cœlum,” “by these steps one climbs to heaven”: heaven itself is forced open to everyone. From universal redemption, through universal justification within a general covenant, they have reached universal salvation. “Haud ignota loquor,” “I am not speaking of things unknown to me.” On this view, no one can forfeit the inheritance that has been purchased.

paragraphs.original: “Quare agite, ô juvenes, tantarum in munere laudum, Cingite fronde comas, et pocula porgite dextris, Communemque vocate Deum, et date vina volentes.”[4]
paragraphs.modern: “Quare agite, ô juvenes, tantarum in munere laudum, Cingite fronde comas, et pocula porgite dextris, Communemque vocate Deum, et date vina volentes.” “Come then, young men, in honour of such great deeds, crown your hair with leaves, hold out cups in your right hands, invoke the god we share, and gladly pour the wine.”[4]

paragraphs.original: “March on, brave youths, i’ th’ praise of such free grace, Surround your locks with bays; and full cups place In your right hands: drink freely on, then call O’ th’ common hope, the ransom general.”
paragraphs.modern: “March on, brave young men, praising such free grace. Crown your heads with laurel and put full cups in your right hands. Drink freely, then call on the hope shared by all: the ransom for everyone.”

paragraphs.original: These and the like persuasions I no way dislike, because wholly new to the men of this generation; that I may add this by the way:— Every age hath its employment in the discovery of truth. We are not come to the bottom of vice or virtue. The whole world hath been employed in the practice of iniquity five thousand years and upwards, and yet “aspice hoc novum” may be set on many villainies. Behold daily new inventions! No wonder, then, if all truth be not yet discovered. Something may be revealed to them who as yet sit by. Admire not if Saul also be among the prophets, for who is their father? Is he not free in his dispensations? Are all the depths of Scripture, where the elephants may swim, just fathomed to the bottom? Let any man observe the progress of the last century in unfolding the truths of God, and he will scarce be obstinate that no more is left as yet undiscovered. Only the itching of corrupted fancies, the boldness of darkened minds and lascivious wanton wits, in venting new-created nothings, insignificant vanities, with an intermixed dash of blasphemy, is that which I desire to oppose; and that especially considering the genius (if I may so speak) of the days wherein we live; in which, what by one means, what by another, there is almost a general deflection after novelty grown amongst us. [5]“Some are credulous, some negligent, some fall into errors, some seek them.” A great suspicion also every day grows upon me, which I would thank any one upon solid grounds to free me from, that pride of spirit, with an Herostratus-like design to grow big in the mouths of men, hath acted many in the conception and publication of some easily-invented false opinions. Is it not to be thought, also, that it is from the same humour possessing many, that every one of them almost strives to put on beyond his companions in framing some singular artifice? To be a follower of others, though in desperate engagements, is too mean an undertaking.
paragraphs.modern: I do not reject these and similar beliefs simply because they are entirely new to people of this generation. Let me add this in passing: every age has its own work to do in discovering truth. We have not reached the limits of either vice or virtue. The whole world has practised wickedness for five thousand years and more, yet many crimes could still bear the label “aspice hoc novum,” “look at this new thing.” We see new inventions every day! It is therefore no surprise if not all truth has yet been discovered. Something may be revealed to people who, so far, have sat listening. Do not be astonished if Saul too is among the prophets. Who is their father? Is God not free in the way he distributes his gifts? Have all the depths of Scripture, deep enough for elephants to swim in, been measured to the bottom? Anyone who considers the last century's progress in explaining God's truths will hardly insist that nothing remains undiscovered. What I oppose is the restless itch of corrupt imaginations, the arrogance of darkened minds, and the loose indulgence of unruly intellects, pouring out newly invented nothings and meaningless vanities mixed with blasphemy. This matters especially because of the character, if I may call it that, of our times. Through one influence or another, a nearly general turning toward novelty has developed among us.[5] “Some are gullible, some careless, some stumble into errors, and some go looking for them.” Every day I also grow more suspicious that spiritual pride has moved many people to invent and publish certain easily devised false opinions. Like Herostratus, they seek to make their names widely talked about. I would thank anyone who could give me sound reasons to dismiss this suspicion. Does not the same disposition seem to explain why almost every one of them tries to outdo his companions by devising some peculiar novelty? Merely following others, even in reckless ventures, is too insignificant an achievement.

paragraphs.original: “Aude[6] aliquod brevibus Gyaris, et carcere dignum, Si vis esse aliquis: probitas laudatur et alget.”[7]
paragraphs.modern: “Aude[6] aliquod brevibus Gyaris, et carcere dignum, Si vis esse aliquis: probitas laudatur et alget.” “Dare to do something deserving exile to tiny Gyarus or imprisonment if you want to be somebody. Honesty receives praise and is left out in the cold.”[7]

paragraphs.original: And let it be no small peccadillo, no underling opinion, friends, if in these busy times you would have it taken notice of. Of ordinary errors you may cry, —
paragraphs.modern: And friends, if you want people to notice it in these busy times, make sure it is no minor fault, no second-rate opinion. Of ordinary errors you may cry:

paragraphs.original: “Quis leget hæc? ― nemo hercule nemo, Vel duo, vel nemo.”[8]
paragraphs.modern: “Quis leget hæc? ― nemo hercule nemo, Vel duo, vel nemo.” “Who will read this? By Hercules, no one, no one! Perhaps two people, or no one.”[8]

paragraphs.original: They must be glorious attainments, beyond the understanding of men, and above the wisdom of the word, which attract the eyes of poor deluded souls. The great shepherd of the sheep, our Lord Jesus Christ, recover his poor wanderers to his own fold! But to return thither from whence we have digressed:—
paragraphs.modern: To attract the eyes of poor, deceived souls, these must be glorious achievements beyond human understanding and above the wisdom of Scripture. May the great shepherd of the sheep, our Lord Jesus Christ, bring his poor wanderers back to his own fold! But let us return to the point from which we digressed:

paragraphs.original: This is that fatal Helena, a useless, barren, fruitless fancy, for whose enthroning such irksome, tedious contentions have been caused to the churches of God; a mere Rome, a desolate, dirty place of cottages, until all the world be robbed and spoiled to adorn it. Suppose Christ died for all, yet if God in his free purpose hath chosen some to obtain life and salvation, passing by others, will it be profitable only to the former, or unto all? Surely the purpose of God must stand, and he will do all his pleasure. Wherefore, election either, with Huberus, by a wild contradiction, must be made universal, or the thoughts of the Most High suspended on the free-will of man. Add this borrowed feather to the general ransom, that at least it may have some colour of pompous ostentation. Yet if the free grace of God work effectually in some, not in others, can those others, passed by in its powerful operation, have any benefit by universal redemption? No more than the Egyptians had in the angel’s passing over those houses whose doors were not sprinkled with blood, leaving some dead behind him. Almighty, powerful, free grace, then, must strike its sail, that free-will, like the Alexandrian ships to the Roman havens, may come in with top and top-gallant; for without it the whole territory of universal redemption will certainly be famished. But let these doctrines of God’s eternal election, the free grace of conversion, perseverance, and their necessary consequents, be asserted, “movet cornicula risum, furtivis nudata colouribus;” it hath not the least appearance of profit or consolation but what it robs from the sovereignty and grace of God. But of these things more afterward.
paragraphs.modern: This is that fatal Helen, the useless, barren, fruitless idea whose enthronement has caused God's churches such wearying, prolonged disputes. It is like Rome, a desolate, filthy settlement of huts until the whole world is robbed and plundered to adorn it. Suppose Christ died for everyone, but God, by his free decision, chose some to receive life and salvation and passed over others. Will Christ's death benefit only the chosen, or everyone? God's purpose must surely stand, and he will do everything he pleases. Consequently, either election must be made universal, as Huberus makes it in a wild contradiction, or the intentions of the Most High must depend on human free will. Add this borrowed feather to universal ransom, so that it at least has some appearance of magnificent display. Yet if God's free grace acts effectively in some people and not in others, can those passed over by its powerful action benefit from universal redemption? No more than the Egyptians benefited when the angel passed through the houses whose doors were not sprinkled with blood and left dead people behind him. Almighty, powerful, free grace must therefore lower its sails so that free will can enter with every sail flying, like the Alexandrian ships entering Roman ports. Without it, the whole realm of universal redemption will certainly starve. But affirm God's eternal election, his free grace in conversion, perseverance, and the necessary consequences of these doctrines, and “movet cornicula risum, furtivis nudata colouribus,” “the little crow provokes laughter when stripped of its stolen colours.” Universal redemption has no appearance of benefit or comfort except what it steals from God's sovereignty and grace. More on these matters later.

paragraphs.original: Some flourishing pretences are usually held out by the abettors of the general ransom; which by thy patience, courteous reader, we will a little view in the entrance, to remove some prejudice that may lie in the way of truth:—
paragraphs.modern: Supporters of a universal ransom commonly put forward several impressive claims. With your patience, courteous reader, we will briefly examine them at the outset, to remove some prejudices that may obstruct the truth:

paragraphs.original: First, The glory of God, they say, is exceedingly exalted by it; his good-will and kindness towards men abundantly manifested in this enlargement of its extent; and his free grace, by others restrained, set out with a powerful endearment. This they say; which is, in effect, “All things will be well when God is contented with that portion of glory which is of our assigning.” The princes of the earth account it their greatest wisdom to varnish over their favours, and to set out with a full mouth what they have done with half a hand; but will it be acceptable to lie for God, by extending his bounty beyond the marks and eternal bounds fixed to it in his word? Change first a hair of your own heads, or add a cubit to your own statures, before you come in with an addition of glory, not owned by him, to the Almighty. But so, for the most part, is it with corrupted nature in all such mysterious things; discovering the baseness and vileness thereof. If God be apprehended to be as large in grace as that is in offence (I mean in respect of particular offenders, for in respect of his he is larger), though it be free, and he hath proclaimed to all that he may do what he will with his own, giving no account of his matters, all shall be well, — he is gracious, merciful, etc; but if once the Scripture is conceived to hold out his sovereignty and free distinguishing grace, suited in its dispensation to his own purpose according to election, he is “immanis, truculentus, diabolo, Tiberio tetrior (horresco referens).” The learned know well where to find this language, and I will not be instrumental to propagate their blasphemies to others. “Si deus homini non placuerit, deus non erit,” said Tertullian of the heathen deities; and shall it be so with us? God forbid! This pride is inbred;[9] it is a part of our corruption to defend it. If we maintain, then, the glory of God, let us speak in his own language, or be for ever silent. That is glorious in him which he ascribes unto himself. Our inventions, though never so splendid in our own eyes, are unto him an abomination, a striving to pull him down from his eternal excellency, to make him altogether like unto us. God would never allow that the will of the creature should be the measure of his honour. The obedience of paradise was to have been regulated. God’s prescription hath been the bottom of his acceptation of any duty ever since he had a creature to worship him. The very heathen knew that that service alone was welcome to God which himself required, and that glory owned which himself had revealed that he would appear glorious in it. Hence, as Epimenides[10] advised the Athenians in a time of danger to sacrifice Θεῷ προσήκοντι, “to him to whom it was meet and due,” — which gave occasion to the altar which Paul saw bearing the superscription of Ἀγνώστῳ Θεῷ, “To the unknown God,” — so Socrates tells us in Plato,[11] that every god will be worshipped τῷ μάλιστα αὐτῷ ἀρέσκοντι τρόπῳ, “in that way which pleaseth best his own mind;” and in Christianity, Hierome sets it down for a rule, that “honos præter mandatum est dedecus,” God is dishonoured by that honour which is ascribed to him beyond his own prescription: and one wittily on the second commandment, “Non imago, non simulachrum damnatur, sed non facies tibi.” Assigning to God any thing by him not assumed is a making to ourselves, a deifying of our own imaginations. Let all men, then, cease squaring the glory of God by their own corrupted principles and more corrupted persuasions. The word alone is to be arbitrator in the things of God; which also I hope will appear, by the following treatise, to hold out nothing in the matter in hand contrary to those natural notions of God and his goodness which in the sad ruins of innocency have been retained. On these grounds we affirm, that all that glory of God which is pretended to be asserted by the general ransom, however it may seem glorious to purblind nature, is indeed a sinful flourish, for the obscuring of that glory wherein God is delighted.
paragraphs.modern: First, they say this teaching greatly exalts God's glory. By extending his goodwill and kindness to more people, it supposedly displays them more fully and presents his free grace, which others restrict, in a powerfully attractive way. In effect, they say, “Everything will be well if God is satisfied with the share of glory we assign him.” Earthly rulers think it wise to embellish their favours, talking at full volume about what they have done only half-heartedly. But will God accept lies told on his behalf, extending his generosity beyond the boundaries and eternal limits established in his word? First change a hair on your own heads or add a cubit to your height before trying to add to the Almighty a glory he does not acknowledge. This, however, is how corrupt human nature generally behaves in such mysteries, revealing its own baseness and wickedness. If God is understood to extend grace as widely as human nature extends wrongdoing, all is well: he is gracious, merciful, and so on. I mean as widely in respect of the particular people who offend, for toward his own people his grace is greater than their offence. Yet grace is free, and God has declared to everyone that he may do what he wishes with his own, without accounting for his actions. But once Scripture is understood to proclaim his sovereignty and his free grace that distinguishes between people, distributed according to his own purpose of election, he becomes, in their words, “immanis, truculentus, diabolo, Tiberio tetrior,” “monstrous, savage, more loathsome than the devil or Tiberius”; “horresco referens,” “I shudder to repeat it.” Learned readers know where this language can be found. I will not help spread these people's blasphemies to others. “Si deus homini non placuerit, deus non erit,” “if a god does not please a human being, he will not be a god,” said Tertullian about the pagan deities. Will it be that way with us? God forbid! This pride is inborn,[9] and defending it is part of our corruption. If we uphold God's glory, then, let us speak in his own language or remain silent for ever. What is glorious in him is what he attributes to himself. Our inventions, however splendid they look to us, are detestable to him. They are an attempt to pull him down from his eternal excellence and make him entirely like ourselves. God has never allowed a creature's will to determine the measure of his honour. Even obedience in paradise had to follow his directions. Ever since he had a creature to worship him, his own command has been the basis on which he accepts any service. Even pagans knew that God welcomes only the service he himself requires and acknowledges only the glory in which he has revealed that he wishes to appear glorious. Thus, in a time of danger, Epimenides[10] advised the Athenians to sacrifice “Θεῷ προσήκοντι,” “to the god to whom it was fitting and due.” This gave rise to the altar Paul saw with the inscription “Ἀγνώστῳ Θεῷ,” “To the unknown God.” Similarly, Socrates tells us in Plato[11] that every god is to be worshipped “τῷ μάλιστα αὐτῷ ἀρέσκοντι τρόπῳ,” “in the way most pleasing to him.” In Christianity, Jerome states the rule “honos præter mandatum est dedecus,” “honour beyond what is commanded is dishonour”: God is dishonoured by honour offered beyond what he has prescribed. Someone has also remarked pointedly about the second commandment, “Non imago, non simulachrum damnatur, sed non facies tibi,” “what is condemned is not simply an image or likeness; the prohibition is, ‘You shall not make one for yourself.’” Attributing to God anything he has not claimed for himself is precisely such a making for ourselves, a turning of our own imaginings into gods. Let everyone therefore stop measuring God's glory by corrupt principles and still more corrupt beliefs. Scripture alone must judge the things of God. I also hope the following treatise will show that, on this subject, Scripture teaches nothing contrary to the natural understanding of God and his goodness that remains amid the sad ruins of our original innocence. On these grounds we maintain that all the glory supposedly upheld by a universal ransom, however glorious it looks to half-blind human nature, is really a sinful display that obscures the glory in which God delights.

paragraphs.original: Secondly, It is strongly pretended that the worth and value of the satisfaction of Christ, by the opposite opinion limited to a few, are exceedingly magnified in this extending of them to all; when, besides what was said before unto human extending of the things of God beyond the bounds by himself fixed unto them, the merit of the death of Christ, consisting in its own internal worth and sufficiency, with that obligation which, by his obedience unto death, was put upon the justice of God for its application unto them for whom he died, is quite enervated and overthrown by it, made of no account, and such as never produced of itself absolutely the least good to any particular soul: which is so fully manifested in the following treatise, as I cannot but desire the reader’s sincere consideration of it, it being a matter of no small importance.
paragraphs.modern: Secondly, they strongly insist that extending Christ's satisfaction for sin to everyone greatly magnifies its worth and value, which the opposing view supposedly confines to a few. But consider what I have already said about human attempts to extend God's works beyond the limits he himself has fixed. Beyond that, this teaching actually weakens and overturns the merit of Christ's death. That merit consists in its own inherent worth and sufficiency, together with the obligation that Christ's obedience to the point of death placed on God's justice to apply it to those for whom he died. Their teaching makes it worthless, something that by itself has never actually secured even the smallest benefit for any particular soul. The following treatise demonstrates this so fully that I must ask the reader to consider it sincerely. It is no small matter.

paragraphs.original: Thirdly, A seeming smile cast upon the opinion of universal redemption by many texts of Scripture, with the ambiguity of some words, which though in themselves either figurative or indefinite, yet seem to be of a universal extent, maketh the abettors of it exceedingly rejoice. Now, concerning this I shall only desire the reader not to be startled at the multitude of places of Scripture which he may find heaped up by some of late about this business (especially by Thomas More, in his “Universality of Free Grace”), as though they proved and confirmed that for which they are produced, but rather prepare himself to admire at the confidence of men, particularly of him now named, to make such a flourish with colours and drums, having indeed no soldiers at all; for, notwithstanding all their pretences, it will appear that they hang the whole weight of their building on three or four texts of Scripture, — namely, 1 Tim. ii. 5, 6; John iii. 16, 17; Heb. ii. 9; 1 John ii. 2, with some few others, — and the ambiguity of two or three words, which themselves cannot deny to be of exceeding various acceptations. All which are at large discussed in the ensuing treatise, no one place that hath with the least show or colour been brought forth by any of our adversaries, in their own defence, or for the opposing of the effectual redemption of the elect only, being omitted, the book of Thomas More being in all the strength thereof fully met withal and enervated.
paragraphs.modern: Thirdly, many Scripture passages seem to look favourably on universal redemption, and certain ambiguous words appear to include everyone, although they are actually figurative or indefinite. This makes its supporters greatly rejoice. On this point, I simply ask readers not to be overwhelmed by the multitude of passages recently piled up by some writers, especially Thomas More in his “Universality of Free Grace,” as though those passages established what they are quoted to prove. Instead, prepare to be astonished at the confidence of these men, especially the one just named, who make such a display of flags and drums when they have no soldiers at all. Despite all their claims, it will become clear that they rest the entire weight of their structure on three or four passages, namely 1 Timothy 2:5–6; John 3:16–17; Hebrews 2:9; and 1 John 2:2, with a few others. They also rely on the ambiguity of two or three words that, as they themselves must admit, carry widely varying meanings. All these matters are discussed at length in the following treatise. I have omitted no passage that any opponent has presented with even the slightest appearance of support, either to defend his position or to oppose the effective redemption of the elect alone. The full force of Thomas More's book is answered and its arguments undermined.

paragraphs.original: Fourthly, Some men have, by I know not what misprision, entertained a persuasion that the opinion of the Universalists serves exceedingly to set forth the love and free grace of God; yea, they make free grace, that glorious expression, to be that alone which is couched in their persuasion, — namely, that “God loves all alike, gave Christ to die for all, and is ready to save all if they will lay hold on him;” — under which notion how greedily the hook as well as the bait is swallowed by many we have daily experience, when the truth is, it is utterly destructive to the free distinguishing grace of God in all the dispensations and workings thereof. It evidently opposeth God’s free grace of election, as hath been declared, and therein that very love from which God sent his Son. His free distinguishing grace, also, of effectual calling must be made by it to give place to nature’s darling, free-will; yea, and the whole covenant of grace made void, by holding it out no otherwise but as a general removing of the wrath which was due to the breach of the covenant of works: for what else can be imagined (though this certainly they have not, John iii. 36) to be granted to the most of those “all” with whom they affirm this covenant to be made? Yea, notwithstanding their flourish of free grace, as themselves are forced to grant, that after all that was effected by the death of Christ, it was possible that none should be saved, so I hope I have clearly proved that if he accomplished by his death no more than they ascribe unto it, it is utterly impossible that any one should be saved. “Quid dignum tanto?”
paragraphs.modern: Fourthly, through some misunderstanding I cannot explain, certain people have become convinced that the teaching of universal redemption displays God's love and free grace especially well. Indeed, they confine that glorious expression, “free grace,” to their own belief: “God loves everyone equally, gave Christ to die for everyone, and is ready to save everyone if they will take hold of him.” We see daily how greedily many swallow the hook along with the bait when the teaching is presented in this form. In truth, however, it completely destroys God's free grace that distinguishes between people, in all its arrangements and actions. As already shown, it clearly opposes God's free grace in election, and therefore the very love that moved God to send his Son. His freely distinguishing grace in effectively calling people must also give way to human nature's darling, free will. Indeed, the whole covenant of grace is emptied of meaning when it is presented merely as a general removal of the wrath deserved for breaking the covenant of works. What else could be imagined as granted to most of the “everyone” with whom they say this covenant is made? Yet certainly they do not even possess that removal of wrath, John 3:36. Furthermore, despite their display of free grace, they themselves must admit that, after everything accomplished by Christ's death, it remained possible that no one would be saved. I hope I have clearly proved something further: if his death accomplished no more than they allow, it is utterly impossible for anyone to be saved. “Quid dignum tanto?” “What result is worthy of such great claims?”

paragraphs.original: Fifthly, The opinion of universal redemption is not a little advantaged by presenting to convinced men a seeming ready way to extricate themselves out of all their doubts and perplexities, and to give them all the comfort the death of Christ can afford before they feel any power of that death working within them, or find any efficacy of free grace drawing their hearts to the embracing of Christ in the promise, or obtaining a particular interest in him; which are tedious things to flesh and blood to attend unto and wait upon. Some boast that, by this persuasion, that hath been effected in an hour which they waited for before seven years without success. To dispel this poor empty flourish, I shall show, in the progress, that it is very ready and apt to deceive multitudes with a plausible delusion, but really undermines the very foundations of that strong unfailing consolation which God hath showed himself abundantly willing that the heirs of promise should receive.
paragraphs.modern: Fifthly, universal redemption gains considerable support by offering people who have become aware of their sin an apparently immediate escape from all their doubts and perplexities. It promises them every comfort Christ's death can offer before they experience any power of that death working within them, or any effective action of free grace drawing their hearts to receive Christ in the promise and to gain a personal share in him. These are things our human nature finds tiresome to attend to and wait for. Some boast that this belief accomplished in an hour what they had previously waited seven unsuccessful years to receive. To dispel this poor, empty boast, I will show as we proceed that the teaching readily deceives multitudes with a plausible illusion. In reality it undermines the very foundations of the strong, unfailing comfort that God has abundantly shown he wants the heirs of his promise to receive.

paragraphs.original: These and the like are the general pretences wherewith the abettors of a general ransom do seek to commend themselves and opinion to the affections of credulous souls; through them making an open and easy passage into their belief, for the swallowing and digesting of that bitter potion which lurks in the bottom of their cup. Of these I thought meet to give the reader a brief view in the entrance, to take off his mind from empty generals, that he might be the better prepared to weigh all things carefully in an equal balance, when he shall come to consider those particulars afterward insisted on, wherein the great strength of our adversaries lies. It remaineth only that I give the Christian reader a brief account of my call unto, and undertaking in, this work, and so close this preface. First, then, I will assure thee it is not the least thirst in my affections to be drinking of the waters of Meribah, nor the least desire to have a share in Ishmael’s portion, to have my hand against others, and theirs against me, that put me upon this task. I never like myself worse than when faced with a vizard of disputing in controversies. The complexion of my soul is much more pleasant unto me in the waters of Shiloah:—
paragraphs.modern: These and similar broad claims are the means by which supporters of a universal ransom try to win the affection of gullible people for themselves and their opinion. Through those affections they gain easy access to people's belief, so that they swallow and digest the bitter medicine hidden at the bottom of the cup. I thought it appropriate to give the reader this brief view at the beginning, to turn attention away from empty generalities. The reader may then be better prepared to weigh everything carefully and fairly when considering the specific arguments developed later, where our opponents' greatest strength lies. All that remains before I close this preface is to give the Christian reader a brief account of what called me to this work and led me to undertake it. First, be assured that I did not take on this task from any thirst to drink the waters of Meribah, the waters of strife, or any wish to share Ishmael's lot, with my hand against others and theirs against me. I never like myself less than when I wear the mask of someone arguing over controversies. I find my soul's appearance much more pleasing in the peaceful waters of Shiloah:

paragraphs.original: “― Nuper me in littore vidi, Cum placidum ventis staret mare.”[12]
paragraphs.modern: “― Nuper me in littore vidi, Cum placidum ventis staret mare.” “Recently I saw my reflection on the shore, when the sea stood calm, undisturbed by winds.”[12]

paragraphs.original: What invitation there can be in itself for any one to lodge, much less abide, in this quarrelsome, scrambling territory, where, as Tertullian[13] says of Pontus, “omne quod flat Aquilo est,” no wind blows but what is sharp and keen, I know not. Small pleasure in those walks which are attended with dangerous precipices and unpleasing difficulties on every side:—
paragraphs.modern: I cannot imagine what attraction this quarrelsome, jostling territory could have in itself to make anyone stop here, much less stay. As Tertullian[13] says of Pontus, “omne quod flat Aquilo est,” “every wind that blows is the north wind”: every breeze is sharp and biting. There is little pleasure in paths bordered on every side by dangerous cliffs and unpleasant difficulties:

paragraphs.original: “Utque viam teneas, nulloque errore traharis; Per tamen adversi gradieris cornua Tauri, Hæmoniosque arcus, violentique ora Leonis.”[14]
paragraphs.modern: “Utque viam teneas, nulloque errore traharis; Per tamen adversi gradieris cornua Tauri, Hæmoniosque arcus, violentique ora Leonis.” “Even if you keep to the path and never stray, you will still pass between the horns of the Bull facing you, past the Thessalian Archer's bow, and the jaws of the fierce Lion.”[14]

paragraphs.original: No quiet nor peace in these things and ways, but continual brawls and dissensions:—
paragraphs.modern: There is no rest or peace in these activities and ways, only continual quarrels and disagreements:

paragraphs.original: “― Non hospes ab hospite tutus, Non socer a genero: fratrum quoque gratia rara est.”[15]
paragraphs.modern: “― Non hospes ab hospite tutus, Non socer a genero: fratrum quoque gratia rara est.” “The guest is not safe from his host, nor the father-in-law from his son-in-law; even affection between brothers is rare.”[15]

paragraphs.original: The strongest bonds of nearest relations are too commonly broken by them. Were it not for that precept, Jude 3, and the like, of “contending earnestly for the faith once delivered unto the saints,” with the sounding of my bowels for the loss of poor seduced souls, I could willingly engage myself into an unchangeable resolution to fly all wordy battles and paper combats for the residue of my few and evil days.
paragraphs.modern: All too often these disputes break the strongest bonds between the closest relations. If it were not for the command in Jude 3 and similar passages to “struggle earnestly for the faith handed down once for all to God's people,” together with my deep anguish over the loss of poor, deceived souls, I would gladly make an unchangeable resolution to avoid every battle of words and war on paper for the rest of my few and troubled days.

paragraphs.original: It is not, then (that I may return), any salamandrian complexion that was the motive to this undertaking. Neither, secondly, was it any conceit of my own abilities for this work, as though I were the fittest among many to undertake it. I know that as in all things I am “less than the least of all saints,” so in these I am
paragraphs.modern: To return to my point, then, I did not undertake this work because I have a salamander's supposed taste for living in fire. Secondly, neither did I imagine my abilities made me better suited than others to attempt it. I know that, just as in everything I am “less than the least of all God's people,” so in these matters I am

paragraphs.original: ― οὔτε τρίτος οὔτε τέταρτος Οὔτε δυωδέκατος οὐδ’ ἐν λόγῳ οὐδ’ ἐν ἀριθμῷ
paragraphs.modern: ― οὔτε τρίτος οὔτε τέταρτος Οὔτε δυωδέκατος οὐδ’ ἐν λόγῳ οὐδ’ ἐν ἀριθμῷ — “neither third nor fourth, nor even twelfth; neither reckoned nor counted at all.”

paragraphs.original: Abler[16] pens have had, within these few years, the discussing and ventilating of some of these questions in our own language. Some have come to my hands, but none of weight, before I had well-nigh finished this heap of mine own, which was some twelve months since and upwards. In some of these, at least, in all of them, I had rested fully satisfied, but that I observed they had all tied up themselves to some certain parts of the controversy, especially the removing of objections, neither compassing nor methodizing the whole; whereby I discerned that the nature of the things under debate, — namely, satisfaction, reconciliation, redemption, and the like, — was left exceedingly in the dark, and the strong foundation of the whole building not so much as once discovered. It was always upon my desires that someone would undertake the main, and unfold out of the word, from the bottom, the whole dispensation of the love of God to his elect in Jesus Christ, with the conveyance of it through the promises of the gospel, being in all the fruits thereof purchased and procured by the oblation and intercession of Jesus Christ; by which it could not but be made apparent what was the great design of the blessed Trinity in this great work of redemption, with how vain an attempt and fruitless endeavour it must needs be to extend it beyond the bounds and limits assigned unto it by the principal agents therein. That arguments also might be produced for the confirmation of the truth we assert, in opposition to the error opposed, and so the weak established and dissenters convinced, was much in my wishes. The doctrine of the satisfaction of Christ, his merit, and the reconciliation wrought thereby, understood aright by few, and of late oppugned by some, being so nearly related to the point of redemption, I desired also to have seen cleared, unfolded, vindicated, by some able pen. But now, after long waiting, finding none to answer my expectation, although of myself I can truly say, with him in the Comedian, “Ego me neque tam astutum esse, neque ita perspicacem id scio,” that I should be fit for such an undertaking, the counsel of the poet also running much in my mind, —
paragraphs.modern: In recent years, more capable writers[16] have discussed and examined some of these questions in our own language. Some of their works reached me, but none of substantial weight did so until I had nearly finished this collection of my own, twelve months or more ago. I would have rested fully satisfied with some of them, or at least with all of them taken together, except that I noticed they all confined themselves to particular aspects of the controversy, especially answering objections. They neither covered the whole subject nor arranged it systematically. As a result, I saw that the nature of the things being debated, satisfaction for sin, reconciliation, redemption, and the like, remained very obscure. The strong foundation of the entire structure had not even been brought to light. I had always wanted someone to address the central issue and explain from Scripture, from its very foundations, the whole way God bestows his love on his elect in Jesus Christ. This would include how that love reaches them through the gospel promises, all its benefits having been purchased and secured by Jesus Christ's offering of himself and his intercession. Such an account would necessarily make clear the blessed Trinity's great purpose in redemption, and how vain and fruitless it is to extend that work beyond the boundaries fixed by its principal agents. I also greatly wished to see arguments presented that would confirm the truth we affirm against the error we oppose, strengthening the weak and persuading those who disagree. Because the doctrines of Christ's satisfaction for sin, his merit, and the reconciliation he accomplished are so closely related to redemption, I wanted some capable writer to clarify, explain, and defend them as well. Few understand them correctly, and some have recently attacked them. But after waiting a long time, I found no one who met my expectation. Of myself I can truly say, with the character in the comic playwright, “Ego me neque tam astutum esse, neque ita perspicacem id scio,” “I know that I am neither so clever nor so perceptive,” as to be suited to such a task. The poet's advice also kept running through my mind:

paragraphs.original: “Sumite materiam vestris, qui scribitis, æquam Viribus; et versate diu, quid ferre recusent, Quid valeant humeri.”[17]
paragraphs.modern: “Sumite materiam vestris, qui scribitis, æquam Viribus; et versate diu, quid ferre recusent, Quid valeant humeri.” “You who write, choose a subject suited to your strength. Consider long and carefully what your shoulders cannot bear and what they can carry.”[17]

paragraphs.original: Yet, at the last, laying aside all such thoughts, by looking up to Him who supplieth seed to the sower, and doth all our works for us, I suffered myself to be overcome unto the work with that of another, “Ab alio quovis hoc fieri mallem quam a me; sed a me tamen potius quam a nemine;” — “I had rather it should have been done by any than myself, of myself only rather than of none;” especially considering the industrious diligence of the opposers of truth in these days:—
paragraphs.modern: At last, however, I set these thoughts aside and looked up to the one who supplies seed to the sower and accomplishes all our works for us. I allowed myself to be persuaded to undertake the work by another person's saying, “Ab alio quovis hoc fieri mallem quam a me; sed a me tamen potius quam a nemine,” “I would rather anyone else did this than I; but I would rather do it myself than have no one do it.” This was especially so when I considered how energetically and diligently people oppose the truth in our day:

paragraphs.original: “Scribimus indocti doctique, ― Ut jugulent homines, surgunt de nocte latrones; Ut teipsum serves non expergisceris?”[18]
paragraphs.modern: “Scribimus indocti doctique, ― Ut jugulent homines, surgunt de nocte latrones; Ut teipsum serves non expergisceris?” “Learned and unlearned alike, we write. Robbers rise at night to murder people; will you not wake up to save yourself?”[18]

paragraphs.original: Add unto the former desire a consideration of the frequent conferences I had been invited unto about these things, the daily spreading of the opinions here opposed about the parts where I live, and a greater noise concerning their prevailing in other places, with the advantage they had obtained by some military abettors, with the stirring up of divers eminent and learned friends, and you have the sum of what I desire to hold forth as the cause of my undertaking this task. What the Lord hath enabled me to perform therein must be left to the judgment of others. Altogether hopeless of success I am not; but fully resolved that I shall not live to see a solid answer given unto it. If any shall undertake to vellicate and pluck some of the branches, rent from the roots and principles of the whole discourse, I shall freely give them leave to enjoy their own wisdom and imaginary conquest. If any shall seriously undertake to debate the whole cause, if I live to see it effected, I shall engage myself, by the Lord’s assistance, to be their humble convert or fair antagonist. In that which is already accomplished by the good hand of the Lord, I hope the learned may find something for their contentment, and the weak for their strengthening and satisfaction; that in all some glory may redound to Him whose it is, and whose truth is here unfolded by the unworthiest labourer in his vineyard,
paragraphs.modern: Add to that desire the frequent discussions on these matters to which I have been invited, the daily spread of the opinions opposed here in the area where I live, and the louder reports of their success elsewhere. Add the advantage they have gained from some supporters in the military and the encouragement of several distinguished, learned friends. Together, these are the reasons I wish to give for undertaking this task. Others must judge what the Lord has enabled me to accomplish. I am not entirely without hope of success, but I am firmly convinced that I will not live to see a sound answer to this work. If anyone chooses to pick at and tear off a few branches, separating them from the roots and principles of the whole discussion, I freely leave them to enjoy their own wisdom and imagined victory. If anyone seriously undertakes to debate the whole case, and I live to see it done, I commit myself, with the Lord's help, to becoming either their humble convert or their fair opponent. In what the Lord's good hand has already enabled me to accomplish, I hope learned readers will find something satisfying, and weaker readers something to strengthen them and resolve their doubts. Through it all, may some glory return to him to whom glory belongs, whose truth is explained here by the most unworthy worker in his vineyard,

paragraphs.original: J. O.

sections.title: Chapter I: In general of the end of the death of Christ, as it is in the Scripture proposed

paragraphs.original: In general of the end of the death of Christ, as it is in the Scripture proposed.
paragraphs.modern: A general account of the purpose of Christ's death as presented in Scripture.

paragraphs.original: By the end of the death of Christ, we mean in general, both, — first, that which his Father and himself intended in it; and, secondly, that which was effectually fulfilled and accomplished by it. Concerning either we may take a brief view of the expressions used by the Holy Ghost:—
paragraphs.modern: By the purpose of the death of Christ, we generally mean first, what his Father and he intended in it; and, secondly, what was effectually fulfilled and accomplished by it. Concerning either, we may take a brief view of the expressions used by the Holy Ghost.

paragraphs.original: I. For the first. Will you know the end wherefore, and the intention wherewith, Christ came into the world? Let us ask himself (who knew his own mind, as also all the secrets of his Father’s bosom), and he will tell us that the “Son of man came to save that which was lost,” Matt. xviii. 11, — to recover and save poor lost sinners; that was his intent and design, as is again asserted, Luke xix. 10. Ask also his apostles, who know his mind, and they will tell you the same. So Paul, 1 Tim. i. 15, “This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.” Now, if you will ask who these sinners are towards whom he hath this gracious intent and purpose, himself tells you, Matt. xx. 28, that he came to “give his life a ransom for many;” in other places called us, believers, distinguished from the world: for he “gave himself for our sins, that he might deliver us from this present evil world, according to the will of God and our Father,” Gal. i. 4. That was the will and intention of God, that he should give himself for us, that we might be saved, being separated from the world. They are his church: Eph. v. 25–27, “He loved the church, and gave himself for it; that he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word, that he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish:” which last words express also the very aim and end of Christ in giving himself for any, even that they may be made fit for God, and brought nigh unto him; — the like whereof is also asserted, Tit. ii. 14, “He gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works.” Thus clear, then, and apparent, is the intention and design of Christ and his Father in this great work, even what it was, and towards whom, — namely, to save us, to deliver us from the evil world, to purge and wash us, to make us holy, zealous, fruitful in good works, to render us acceptable, and to bring us unto God; for through him “we have access into the grace wherein we stand” Rom. v. 2.
paragraphs.modern: I. For the first point, do you want to know the purpose for and intent with which Christ came into the world? Let us ask the One who knew his mind and all the secrets of his Father’s heart. He will tell us that the “Son of man came to save what was lost,” Matthew 18:11, to recover and save poor lost sinners. That was his intent and his design, as it is again asserted in Luke 19:10. Ask also his apostles, who know his mind, and they will tell you the same. So Paul says in 1 Timothy 1:15, “This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.” Now, if you ask who these sinners are towards whom he has this gracious intent and purpose, Christ himself tells you in Matthew 20:28, that he came to “give his life a ransom for many.” In other places, these sinners are called believers, as distinguished from the world. For he “gave himself for our sins, that he might deliver us from this present evil world, according to the will of God and our Father,” Galatians 1:4. That was the will and intention of God, that Christ would give himself for us, that we might be saved, being separated from the world. They are his church: Ephesians 5:25-27, “He loved the church, and gave himself for it; that he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word, that he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it would be holy and without blemish.” These last words also express the very aim and end of Christ in giving himself for anyone. He did it so that they may be made fit for God, and brought near to him. A like assertion is made in Titus 2:14: “He gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify to himself a special people, zealous of good works.” Thus the intention and design of Christ and his Father in this great work are clear and apparent. We know what it was, and towards whom it was directed, namely, to save us. It was to deliver us from the evil world, to purge and wash us, to make us holy, zealous, fruitful in good works, to render us acceptable, and to bring us to God. For through him “we have access into the grace in which we stand.” Romans 5:2.

paragraphs.original: II. The effect, also, and actual product of the work itself, or what is accomplished and fulfilled by the death, blood-shedding, or oblation of Jesus Christ, is no less clearly manifested, but is as fully, and very often more distinctly, expressed; — as, first, Reconciliation with God, by removing and slaying the enmity that was between him and us; for “when we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son,” Rom. v. 10. “God was in him reconciling the world unto himself, not imputing their trespasses unto them,” 2 Cor. v. 19; yea, he hath “reconciled us to himself by Jesus Christ,” verse 18. And if you would know how this reconciliation was effected, the apostle will tell you that “he abolished in his flesh the enmity, the law of commandments consisting in ordinances; for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace; and that he might reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby,” Eph. ii. 15, 16: so that “he is our peace,” verse 14. Secondly, Justification, by taking away the guilt of sins, procuring remission and pardon of them, redeeming us from their power, with the curse and wrath due unto us for them; for “by his own blood he entered into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us” Heb. ix. 12. “He redeemed us from the curse, being made a curse for us,” Gal. iii. 13; “his own self bearing our sins in his own body on the tree,” 1 Pet. ii. 24. We have “all sinned, and come short of the glory of God;” but are “justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God hath set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins” Rom. iii. 23–25: for “in him we have redemption through his blood, even the forgiveness of sins,” Col. i. 14. Thirdly, Sanctification, by the purging away of the uncleanness and pollution of our sins, renewing in us the image of God, and supplying us with the graces of the Spirit of holiness: for “the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself to God, purgeth our consciences from dead works that we may serve the living God,” Heb. ix. 14; yea, “the blood of Jesus Christ cleanseth us from all sin,” 1 John i. 7. “By himself he purged our sins,” Heb. i. 3. To “sanctify the people with his own blood, he suffered without the gate,” chap. xiii. 12. “He gave himself for the church to sanctify and cleanse it, that it should be holy and without blemish,” Eph. v. 25–27. Peculiarly amongst the graces of the Spirit, “it is given to us,” ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ, “for Christ’s sake, to believe on him,” Phil. i. 29; God “blessing us in him with all spiritual blessings in heavenly places,” Eph. i. 3. Fourthly, Adoption, with that evangelical liberty and all those glorious privileges which appertain to the sons of God; for “God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, to redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons,” Gal. iv. 4, 5. Fifthly, Neither do the effects of the death of Christ rest here; they leave us not until we are settled in heaven, in glory and immortality for ever. Our inheritance is a “purchased possession,” Eph. i. 14: “And for this cause he is the mediator of the new testament, that by means of death, for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first testament, they which are called might receive the promise of eternal inheritance,” Heb. ix. 15. The sum of all is, — The death and blood-shedding of Jesus Christ hath wrought, and doth effectually procure, for all those that are concerned in it, eternal redemption, consisting in grace here and glory hereafter.
paragraphs.modern: II. The effect and actual product of the work itself is no less clearly manifested than its intent. What is accomplished and fulfilled by the death, blood-shedding, or offering of Jesus Christ, is just as fully expressed, and very often more distinctly. First, God reconciles us to himself by removing and slaying the enmity that was between him and us. For “when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son,” Romans 5:10. “God was in him reconciling the world to himself, not imputing their trespasses to them,” 2 Corinthians 5:19. He has “reconciled us to himself by Jesus Christ,” 2 Corinthians 5:18. If you want to know how this reconciliation was effected, the apostle will tell you that “he abolished in his flesh the enmity, the law of commandments consisting in ordinances, to make one new man in himself from two, so making peace; and that he might reconcile both to God in one body by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby,” Ephesians 2:15, 16: so that “he is our peace,” Ephesians 2:14. Secondly, Christ justifies us by taking away the guilt of our sins, procuring remission and pardon for them. He redeems us from their power, along with the curse and wrath that are due to us for them. For “by his own blood he entered into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us,” Hebrews 9:12. “He redeemed us from the curse, being made a curse for us,” Galatians 3:13; “he himself bearing our sins in his own body on the tree,” 1 Peter 2:24. We have “all sinned, and come short of the glory of God;” but are “justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God has set forth to be a propitiation through faith in his blood, to declare his righteousness for the remission of sins,” Romans 3:23-25. For “in him we have redemption through his blood, even the forgiveness of sins,” Colossians 1:14. Thirdly, The Holy Spirit sanctifies us by purging away the uncleanness and pollution of our sins, renewing in us the image of God, and supplying us with the graces of the Spirit of holiness.
